Messages.Author: Steve Bucy
Messages.Body:
This one came up last night in one of our games. We had someone playing
Gangrel put out a bunch of Raptors (eventually 7) and Heidleberg Castle to
move them around. He eventually had all seven on one vamp with superior
Protean. He then Bums Rushes, making the guy rushed loose his entire hand.
He then plays Form of the Mist. The victim redraws, looses his hand again,
and the attacker plays Form of the Mist again. Is this legal? Can he keep
playing Form of the Mist to repeat the combat until he runs out of them?

Steve Bucy

I'd be better off undead...

Messages.Author: L. Scott Johnson
Messages.Body:
Steve Bucy wrote:
>
> This one came up last night in one of our games. We had someone playing
> Gangrel put out a bunch of Raptors (eventually 7) and Heidleberg Castle to
> move them around. He eventually had all seven on one vamp with superior
> Protean. He then Bums Rushes, making the guy rushed loose his entire hand.
> He then plays Form of the Mist. The victim redraws, looses his hand again,

> and the attacker plays Form of the Mist again. Is this legal? Can he keep
> playing Form of the Mist to repeat the combat until he runs out of them?
>

Before I answer the question of legality, allow me to make an
observation: Since Raptor is a Sabbat card, the Sabbat rules hold -
namely the rule on forced withdrawal when your library is empty and
you have less than a full hand on your untap.

So, this method (if legal) will merely result in the forced withdrawal
of the Rushed minion's controller - not in a victory point for any
Methuselah.

The legality of Form of Mist on a non-blocked action is under dispute.
An old Rules Team ruling says that it is allowable, but recently
someone (Thomas?) pointed out that this is not legal under the rules
of gaining stealth (you cannot gain stealth unless you need stealth).

So, we're still waiting on the resolution on that question.

Until then, the old RT holds - and FoM can be played repeatedly on
the same (unblocked or blocked) action.

--
L. Scott Johnson (vte...@regency.wizards.com)
Official VtES Net.Rep for Wizards of the Coast.
(*) - Subject to review by Rules Team

Messages.Body:
LSJ wrote:
"Following that logic: the method of Prisci voting is an optional rule;
the fact that any titled Sabbat vampires have votes at all is optional;
denying Sabbat vampires rank in the Camarilla (Primogen, Prince, etc.) is
optional; denying Camarilla vampires rank in the Sabbat is optional; etc."

Yes, but all of the above mentioned rules are new rules that replace
nothing and simply add new (minor) aspects to the game (much like brand
new cards). The Forced Withdraw rule is a new rule that replaces a
perfectly acceptable pre exisiting rule, and for no good reason. There
was no pre exisiting "Prisci" rule that has been eraticated and replaced,
nor do the Prisci have any great effect on the structure of the game as a
whole (or any other of the above mentioned rules). They are basically new
"Flavor" rules. The Forced Withdraw rule substantially changes the rules
of the game as a whole. Originaly, if you ran out of cards, you continued
to play. Now if you run out of cards, you lose. This is a very
substantial difference, and a very good reason why one would opt not to
use this rule.

The use of the expansion does (at least for the cases I state - and
possibly extending to the Withdrawal rule).

So the withdrawal rule is optional. OK. Obviously, this implementation
needs a little clarification.

Currently, official tournaments which allow Sabbat cards (i.e.,
non-restricted tourneys, i.e. all of them that I know of) will
be using this withdrawal rule due to the nature of how rules

more quickly than the rest of the decks.

the decks I see winning lately. Speed cycling combat decks don't
seem too punished so far.

Such a deck would be reduced to a speedbump for its predator once
the library is exhausted in most cases; so I doubly cannot agree
that this is "further" punishment. The deck has its reward,
regardless of the withdrawl rule in use.

Messages.Author: ni...@rci.rogers.com
Messages.Body:
>This one came up last night in one of our games. We had someone playing
>Gangrel put out a bunch of Raptors (eventually 7) and Heidleberg Castle to

>move them around. He eventually had all seven on one vamp with superior
>Protean. He then Bums Rushes, making the guy rushed loose his entire hand.
>He then plays Form of the Mist. The victim redraws, looses his hand again,

>and the attacker plays Form of the Mist again. Is this legal? Can he keep
>playing Form of the Mist to repeat the combat until he runs out of them?

Ok, so I'm not LSJ.... but I'll answer anyway.

This is my take on the situation:

Superior Form of Mist only continues the action if there is an action to
continue.

As soon as the acting minion enters combat with the chosen target, the Bum's
Rush action is considered successful. Playing superior Form of Mist during the
ensuing combat will not continue the Bum's Rush action because it has already
resolved.

If, however, the Bum's Rush action had been blocked, the acting minion could
play superior Form of Mist to allow it to continue to Rush the original target.

Messages.Author: James Hamblin
Messages.Body:
L. Scott Johnson wrote:
>

> > punishes decks which go through cards quickly (like combat decks), and

> more quickly than the rest of the decks.
>
> Whether this is "further" punishment is questionable, considering
> the decks I see winning lately. Speed cycling combat decks don't
> seem too punished so far.

Well, considering the "unit of success" of each type of deck:

Vote: Successful Vote. Cost: ~2 cards: vote card, extra votes.
Bleed: Successful Bleed. Cost: ~3 cards: bleed card, +bleed/+stealth.
Combat: Successful Combat. Cost: ~6 cards: rush card, maneuver(s),
strikes, presses, etc.

So Combat cycles its cards much faster than either of the other major
strategies, and on top of that, a successful combat does not cause
direct pool loss, whereas Vote/Bleed does. So when I say that combat is
punished I mean that it is harder to win (fulfill victory conditions)
with a combat deck.

Now, under the new Sabbat rules, combat is hurt by being forced out of
the game prematurely. I myself have ousted people long after I ran out
of cards, and I do not agree with the rule.

> Such a deck would be reduced to a speedbump for its predator once
> the library is exhausted in most cases; so I doubly cannot agree
> that this is "further" punishment. The deck has its reward,
> regardless of the withdrawl rule in use.

Not necessarily. The following situation happens fairly often:

2 players left: the combat deck and some other deck. The combat deck is
cruising along, torporizing the other players vampires. The combat deck
has 4 ready minions, the other deck has 1. Both players have not too
much pool. The combat deck runs out of cards. Under the old withdraw
rules, the combat deck would get two more victory points; you don't need
cards to win in this situation. Under the new rule, the combat deck
gets _no_ VPs and the other deck gets one!

Messages.Author: PDB6
Messages.Body:
LSJ wrote:
"As an aside, running out of pool will oust you in a worse manner than
running out of cards. Is this a good reason to consider this rule on
ousting a bad rule?"

Now that was just silly :-)

My point is that originally if you ran out of cards, you still had the
option of continuing to play. Now you do not, which is a very substantial
and unneeded rules change. Getting ousted by running out of pool was a
rule with which the game was designed, just like continuing to play when
you ran out of cards was a rule with which the game was designed. If, for
instance, a rule was developed for the Sabbat expansion that said "Now,
instead of being ousted when you run out of pool, you may continue to play
until you run out of cards.", it would be just as rediculous as the Forced
Withdraw rule.

Yes, card managment is an important part of Jyhad, and always has been,
but in the basic set and the first 2 expansions, there was no need to
worry about running out of cards, other than the basic problem of having
no more cards. Granted, the original Withdaw rule was very unweildy and
close to impossible, but WOtC could have very easily come up with a new
Withdraw rule (perhaps if when you ran out of cards, you could choose to
Withdraw and get no points, but if you wished to continue, you still had
that option) that did not change a very basic and important rule, i.e.
that even if you ran out of cards, you could continue to play. I have
seen many many games won by players who have run out of cards, be it on
the very next turn after they have run out, or many turns afterwords.
Sure, sometimes they become speed bumbs, but very often a player in a
great position runs out of cards in the end game but still can win with
what they have in play.

Messages.Author: PDB6
Messages.Body:
LSJ wrote:
" So the rule is different, but it's hardly the game-breaker that it's
being made out to be."

I would never really claim that the Forced Withdraw rule is a real
game-breaker, as more often than not it will never come up, but what it is
is another example of a bad idea by the people left in charge of designing
this game.

Originally, when you ran out of cards you could either contiunue to play
(possibly to win) or attempt to withdraw, which was close to impossible.
Now you must withdraw, whether you were about to win or not. You have no
choice when you are out of cards. You could stop playing cards when you
get down to your last one to avoid being Forced to Withdraw, turning the
"Forced Withdraw" rule into the "Forced Seven Card Smaller Deck" rule.

I'm not quite sure what the intention of this rule was, but what ever it
was, it was a bad idea. If it was to make Withdrawing easier, sure, it
did that but at the great cost of _having_ to Withdraw, which is a far cry
from the original intention of the Withdraw rule. If the intention of the
Forced Withdraw rule was to make Jyhad just that much closer to Magic, ok,
it did that, but that was a bad thing ("Yaa! Now I can win by "Decking"
other players! Woo Hoo!"). If the intention was to impose a stiff
penalty for poor card management, then it failed, as you can always just
not play any of your last seven cards (unless you are facing a deck that
can "Deck" you with Dr. Jest or Raptors...), avoiding the whole thing. If
it was intended as a rule to "punish" high speed card cycle decks, then it
was completely unnecessary, as these decks are no better than any other
decks.

As it is so easy to avoid ever actually running out of cards (just by not
playing any of your last seven), it seems fairly pointless to have a
_Forced_ rule, as you are never actually _Forced_ to Withdraw, unless
someone "Decks" you. As a result, the _Forced_ part of the Withdraw rule
serves little purpose other than to effectively reduce all deck sizes by
seven, and to open up the wack world of "Decking" opponents, which is very
far from the original rule design.

I would suggest that the Forced Withdraw rule be changed to something
along the lines of:

"If you start a turn with less than seven cards in your hand and have no
cards in your library, you _may_ withdraw from the Jyhad. If you
Withdraw, you gain no VPs, nor does your Predator gain a VP or six pool as
a result. You are never _required_ to Withdraw."

This would result in:

A) Fixing the nigh-impossible original Withdrawing rules, while
maintaining the spirit of those rules.
B) Making "Decking" someone impossible.
C) Allowing players in a good position who run out of cards to continue
to play, as in the original rules.
D) Making a great deal of long time Jyhad players happy.

Peter D Bakija

Messages.Author: James Hamblin
Messages.Body:
L. Scott Johnson wrote:
>
> Again, if the "speed-cycle" combat deck finds itself in a position near
> the end of the game to win without playing cards (!?),

Is this to indicate that you have never come upon this situation?

> then it should
> stop playing cards as soon as it draws it's last one. It will have the
> same effect (unless someone has a Raptor out and the combat deck failed
> to kill the Raptor - which would be a mistake on the combat deck's part,
> knowing that it's weakness is card supply.)

First of all, only long range combat decks (pitch or guns) can actually
kill retainers. So a close range Nosferatu, Gangrel or Brujah deck is
SOL? Even without the Raptor, this effectively reduces a deck's size by
7. Depending on which cards you play, there will be some 7 cards which
you will never be able to play.

There are other games with the "you run out of cards, you lose" rule,
but in both of these games that I play (Shadowfist and Magic), there is
no automatic replenishment of cards. Subsequently, both of these games
have card management ("card advantage") as a high priority for success.
In Shadowfist, since you almost always draw up to maximum hand size at
the beginning of turns, this is not such a big issue, but cards that
increase that hand size are very popular. In Jyhad, every time you play
a card, you replace that card. Your hand is a vital resource that is
always present. This is why cards such as Thoughts Betrayed so badly
break the paradigm of the game: they remove your hand from the game,
however temporarily.

Jyhad is not a game of Mind Twists and Curtains of Fullness. Having a
"run out of cards = lose" rule is completely counter to the design of
the game. Your defense of the rule: "well, just stop playing cards as
soon as you draw your last one" is reminiscent of some defenses of TB,
like "well, just use equipment" and "it's just temporary".

> So the rule is different, but it's hardly the game-breaker that it's
> being made out to be.

Being punished for having high card throughput is fairly game-breaking.
High throughput is its own punishment; once you run out of cards, I
agree that it is difficult to win a game. But a player should not be
forced to lose the game for playing too many cards. That's not the way
this game is built.

Just like it is difficult to withdraw under the old withdrawal rule, but
it is possible; I've done it with a combat deck. Why do away with this
old rule?

Here's the RT ruling:

From: aa...@cats.ucsc.edu (Thomas R Wylie)
Newsgroups: rec.games.trading-cards.jyhad
Subject: VTES Rules Team Rulings: 10/17/95
Date: 17 Oct 1995 05:39:07 GMT

1) You may continue an action that has already been considered successful.
For example, if a Bum's Rush is successful, you may play superior Form of
Mist during that combat to continue the action, in which case a second
combat may start (but the action can then be blocked). Note that if you
complete the action again, you get all of its effects again. For example,
if you complete Bum's Rush again, you would get an optional maneuver in the
second combat.

Messages.Author: James Hamblin

Werner Arend wrote:

> around it:
>
> - don't limit deck size
> (if someone wants to play with 120 cards, why not?)

The problem with this is the following: since Jyhad has the automatic
replace rule, given an effective 80 card deck, you can make an effective
160 card deck by simply shuffling together two copies of the deck. This
new deck will be just as effective as the original, but will have the
advantage that each card will be able to be used twice, and it will not
run out of cards until twice as much time has passed.

So, the size of a deck would depend only on the number of cards owned by
a person ("Damn, I only have 27 Undead Strengths. I guess my Brujah
deck will only have 270 cards in it."). The maximum deck size limit is
something that doesn't need tinkering with.

BTW: Does anyone ever find themselves in a situation where someone comes
into a game with a deck which is too big? I mean really big, like
120-150 cards. Do you say anything?

> - impose a 3-card limit
> (no more 7 Raptors)

CL would cause many more problems, and the problem with the FWR is the
rule itself, not Raptor.

> - don't use the rule

Ding! Ding! Ding! This is my point. The rule is not needed, not
useful, and wrong. My group doesn't use it, and I get the impression
that a lot of people don't.

I've _never_ played in an environment where a maximum deck size is
actually enforced. We're well aware that there is a maximum deck size in
the rules, but we're much too lazy to enforce it (the fact that it depends
on the number of players is probably the real reason why we don't use it; we
never know in advance how many players will be at the table, and it can be
anywhere from 3 to 7).

In fact, the average deck size in my various play groups is probably over
100 cards. I think one of my current decks is a bit over 120 cards. It's never
been a problem; maybe we'll change that if we feel the need for it.

As for the forced withdrawal rule... we use it, but we're aware that it sucks.
Usually a player with no cards left will simply stop using them, and nobody
tried to play the Raptor game (though I did it once, involuntarily, in a
Sabbat-only 6-booster game: my prey was finally forced to either let me bleed
or face a Raptor and withdraw from the game...).

I don't agree with you here, because of the following points:
- it's hard to design multi-strategy decks with less than about 100 cards,
and I think that multi-strategy decks are much more interesting than the
more single-minded ones.
- I don't think that running out of cards or not should be able to decide
who wins a victory point. If I lose because I made the wrong deck for the
purpose, or because my predator simply played a better strategy, or because
I don't own some cards that would've turned the table, thats OK, but losing
because running out of cards is boring. This punishes decks with high card
throughput, and increases the value of equipment cards to a degree
where it also becomes boring, because everyone tends to use the same
equipment....
My point is, keep the game interesting by keeping balance between different
types of decks. Encourage players to vary! Limiting Library size to
40+10/player doesn't do that (perhaps 40+15/player would do it better).
The same point goes for a card limit. Depending on 2 or 3 cards for your
strategy may be effective, but it's also rather boring...

> BTW: Does anyone ever find themselves in a situation where someone comes
> into a game with a deck which is too big? I mean really big, like
> 120-150 cards. Do you say anything?

I've seen this twice for sure, and I suspect more often than that (I usually
don't count my opponents' cards). Effective use of a Fragment of the Book of
Nod will reduce your library stack rather quickly. I once got to the bottom
of my 100card deck this way...
